title: How Schoolhouse Rock Rocked: Featuring Bob Nastanovich of Pavement
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of Schoolhouse Rock, the ABC Saturday morning educational cartoon series of animated songs. They cover its origins in early-1970s advertising agency McCaffrey and McCall, the multiplication-table song "Three Is a Magic Number" by jazz musician Bob Dorough, and the seasons on math, grammar, history/America Rock, science, and the computer-themed fifth season. They trace the 1990s revival (Schoolhouse Rock Rocks CD, Money Rock season), stage and parody afterlife, and criticism of the history episodes. The episode closes with a listener mail segment featuring Pavement drummer Bob Nastanovich discussing Pavement's cover of "No More Kings" for the Schoolhouse Rock Rocks album.

segments.title: Opening banter and nostalgia for Schoolhouse Rock
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about growing up with Schoolhouse Rock and the appeal of 1970s childhood nostalgia, and mention that an article on the topic was prompted by listener suggestions.

segments.title: Origins: David McCall and McCaffrey and McCall
segments.summary: David McCall, co-owner of the ad agency McCaffrey and McCall, wanted his son to learn multiplication tables after hearing him sing a Rolling Stones song. The idea of teaching with advertising techniques led to jingle writers and then to Bob Dorough, who insisted on not writing down to kids.

segments.title: Development of the first songs and the ABC deal
segments.summary: The idea was tested with the Bank Street College of Education, art director Tom Yohe developed storyboards, and the pitch to ABC and Michael Eisner led to the show's start in January 1973 with Three Is a Magic Number and other early songs.

segments.title: Multiplication Rock, first season and Bob Dorough
segments.summary: The early series was first conceived as an album called Multiplication Rock, then themed by season. Dorough wrote most songs and sang them, with Grady Tate and Blossom Dearie contributing two. Dorough was nominated for a Grammy and the cast stayed together for the run.

segments.title: Grammar Rock and Lynn Ahrens
segments.summary: Grammar Rock ran in 1973 to 1974 with Conjunction Junction sung by Jack Sheldon. The hosts discuss the sophisticated rhyme and meter, the funk of Verb: That's What's Happening, and secretary-turned-songwriter Lynn Ahrens, who wrote many songs including Interplanet Janet.

segments.title: America Rock and the bicentennial
segments.summary: History Rock, or America Rock, tied into the bicentennial and included No More Kings and Mother Necessity. The hosts discuss the bicentennial's cultural resurgence.

segments.title: Science Rock, I'm Just a Bill, and lobbyist interest
segments.summary: Science Rock followed in 1979, including Interplanet Janet and Telegraph Line. Hosts discuss I'm Just a Bill, a hit that reportedly drew requests from lobbyists and legislators.

segments.title: Season five computers, the 1980s revival, and later revivals
segments.summary: The fifth season, about computers, reversed the creative process so assignments came before songs, and the hosts say it was less successful. After reruns, a 1989 petition led to a return with Money Rock and new episodes. Later the show was revived in stage productions, a 1997 anniversary VHS, a Kennedy Center sing-along, and parodies such as Conspiracy Rock on Saturday Night Live.

segments.title: Criticism of the history episodes and Rufus Xavier Sasaparilla
segments.summary: The hosts discuss criticism of the America Rock episodes, such as Elbow Room, for omitting Native Americans and whitewashing history. They wonder whether schools still mislead children and close with a favorite song, Rufus Xavier Sasaparilla.

segments.title: Bob Nastanovich interview on Pavement's No More Kings
segments.summary: Pavement drummer Bob Nastanovich joins by phone to describe recording Pavement's cover of No More Kings for the Schoolhouse Rock Rocks album, a session organized through Jackie Ferry, its supervisor, and recorded in one take with Steve West. He also discusses Pavement's approach to covers and his outsider role in the band.
